# Four Hundred and Twelve

I have seen her four hundred and twelve times.

I know because I started counting in the second week, when I realized she was going to be a fixture, like the cracked tile at the Delmore stop or the driver who hums show tunes on Thursdays. I keep the count in the notes app on my phone, under a file labeled "Groceries" in case anyone ever looks. Nobody ever looks.

She gets on at Fairview, three stops after me, at 7:22. She sits in the fourth row on the left if it's open, which it usually is, because the fourth row on the left has a heater vent that runs too hot and most people learn to avoid it. She doesn't seem to mind. She carries a green umbrella every single day, including the cloudless ones, including the August week when the pavement softened and the whole city smelled like tar. She reads paperbacks with the covers torn off. I have never been able to tell what they are.

I want to be clear that this is not a romance. I'm fifty-three. I've been married, and then not married, and I have a daughter in Portland who calls on Sundays and tells me about her sourdough starter, which she has named Gerald. I'm not looking for anything. It's just that when you take the same bus for two years, at the same hour, in the same gray light, you start to need the landmarks. You start to organize your mornings around them. The humming driver. The tile. The woman with the green umbrella.

In November, she stopped getting on.

The first day, I didn't think much of it. People get sick. People take vacations. On the third day, I found myself leaning forward at Fairview, watching the doors fold open onto nobody, and I felt something I can only describe as a skipped stair. That small, stupid lurch of the body expecting something solid and finding air.

By the second week I was making up stories. She had moved. She had changed jobs. She had bought a car, finally tired of the heater vent. She had died — I didn't let myself think that one for long, but it came around, the way those thoughts do at 7:22 in the morning when the sky hasn't decided what it's going to be.

The ridiculous thing is that I didn't know her name. I didn't know where she went after the bus. She got off at Harmon Street, near the hospital and the community college and a dozen office buildings, any one of which could have been hers. I had spent four hundred and twelve mornings with her, and I could not have described her to a police officer beyond "fifties, maybe, gray coat, green umbrella, reads books without covers."

I told my daughter about it on a Sunday. I don't know why. She was telling me that Gerald had developed a strange smell and she was worried he'd gone bad, and I just said it, in the middle of her sentence: "There's a woman on my bus who stopped coming."

There was a pause on the line.

"Did you know her?"

"No," I said. "Not at all."

"Then why does it matter?"

I didn't have an answer. I still don't, really. The best I could do was: "Because I was keeping track."

My daughter, who is kinder than I raised her to be, didn't laugh. She said, "Dad, that's kind of beautiful," and then, "also kind of weird," and then she went back to Gerald.

What I didn't tell her was that I'd started getting off at Harmon Street. Just walking around for ten minutes before catching the next bus to my actual stop and arriving late to work. I'd walk past the hospital entrance. The college. The coffee place with the chalkboard sign that always had a pun on it. I told myself I was getting exercise. I did this for six days and felt like a fool on every one of them.

On the nineteenth day, she got on at Fairview.

She had a cast on her right arm, bright blue, the kind they give children. The green umbrella was hooked over her left wrist. She paid awkwardly, fumbling her card with the wrong hand, and the driver — it was a Thursday, the humming one — said something to her I couldn't hear, and she laughed. She walked to the fourth row on the left and sat down beside the too-hot vent and let out a breath, like she'd come home.

I don't know what came over me. I've gone over it many times since. I think it was the cast — the evidence that something had happened, that she had a life with falls in it, with emergency rooms and X-rays and people who signed their names on plaster. I stood up. I walked two rows forward, holding the rail, and sat across the aisle from her.

"You were gone," I said.

She looked at me. She had gray eyes, which I hadn't known. I'd only ever seen her in profile.

"Nineteen days," she said.

I must have looked startled, because she smiled — not unkindly — and lifted the blue cast an inch off her lap.

"Ice," she said. "Front steps. Very undignified." Then: "You're the man in the second row on the right. With the brown scarf. You always get on before me."

"Yes," I said.

"You check your phone at Delmore. Every day. Like you're writing something down."

I thought of the file labeled "Groceries." Four hundred and twelve.

"I suppose I was," I said.

She nodded, as if this were perfectly reasonable, as if everyone kept records of the people who sat around them on the bus, as if that were simply what you did to stay tethered to a morning.

"I'm Ruth," she said.

"Walter."

We didn't say much else. The bus hummed and the driver hummed and the heater vent pushed its dry, too-warm air over both of us. At Harmon Street she stood, and hooked the umbrella over her good wrist, and said, "See you tomorrow, Walter," the way you'd say it to someone you had known for years.

That night I opened the file on my phone. I looked at the number for a long time. Then I changed the title from "Groceries" to "Ruth," and I added one more.

Four hundred and thirteen.
